sections.h2: How does a Texas property go to a tax sale?
sections.html:
A tax lien attaches to every Texas property on January 1 to secure that year's taxes, and an unpaid bill can lead to a lawsuit and a foreclosure auction. The sale is a tax foreclosure auction, and the winning bidder receives a deed afterward.

The ladder runs in order: delinquency notices, an optional installment plan, then a suit by the taxing unit, with court costs added to the bill. Taxes become delinquent on February 1 in most cases. The Comptroller explains that the collector adds a 6 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest at once; the penalty reaches 12 percent on July 1, while interest keeps accruing monthly. Attorneys the unit hires may tack on as much as 20 percent more.

sections.h2: Who runs the sale and where is it held?
sections.html:
Tax foreclosure sales are auctions, typically run by the constable or an agent the taxing unit hires. There is no statewide list of upcoming sales.

The State Law Library tells buyers and owners to check the county clerk or county tax office websites for sale notices. Because each taxing unit and county handles notices its own way, call the tax office that bills the property instead of trusting a general list. The lien survives a change of ownership, so a buyer at an ordinary sale who skips the tax check can end up with the liability.

sections.h2: Can the former owner get the property back after a Texas tax sale?
sections.html:
Yes, in a limited window, and the cost depends on the kind of property. Tax Code Section 34.21 governs redemption, as a Texas Supreme Court opinion explains.

Redemption rules for land sold at a tax sale, as described by the Texas Supreme Court
Property typeRedemption periodPremium
Homestead, agricultural or mineral interestTwo years after the buyer's deed is filed25 percent in the first year, 50 percent in the second
Other property180th day after the deed is filedNot over 25 percent

Source: Texas Supreme Court opinion on Tax Code Section 34.21.

The owner also repays the bid, the deed recording fee, taxes, penalties, interest and costs. The purchaser must itemize those costs within 10 days of a written request, so a redeeming owner should put the request on paper.

sections.h2: Who gets the money when a property sells for more than the taxes owed?
sections.html:
Money left over once the tax debt and costs are paid is called excess proceeds, and the former owner has two years from the sale to claim them. Sections 34.03 and 34.04 of the Tax Code govern the process, according to the State Law Library.

If you suspect money is waiting for you, contact the court that ordered the sale and the tax office. Keep proof of your ownership and your current mailing address with your claim. Heirs of a deceased owner should be ready to show how they inherited, since the claim follows the same ownership questions that arise in probate.

sections.h2: What should a buyer check before bidding at a tax sale?
sections.html:
A buyer should confirm what the deed will and will not do, because the redemption right can reopen the deal after the sale.

  • Ask the tax office which taxing units' taxes are included in the sale.
  • Check whether the property is a homestead, farmland or has a mineral interest, since these have the longer redemption period.
  • Review the county records for other liens. The comptroller files state tax liens with the county clerk, who records them in the state tax lien book.
  • Plan for the possibility of an occupant. A buyer facing an occupant may need an eviction case.

The county clerk is the county recorder, so the clerk's office is also where the deed will be recorded afterward.

sections.h2: How can an owner avoid a tax sale in Texas?
sections.html:
Pay before the delinquency date or work out a payment plan. Some collectors allow installment plans up to 36 months, and one is required on a residence homestead.

Penalty and interest can be waived in many cases if the tax is paid by the 21st day after the owner learns of the delinquency and the waiver is requested in writing before the 181st day after the delinquency date. Older or disabled homeowners can split delinquent tax into four installments, and veterans with a disability rating may qualify for an exemption. Texas school districts apply a $140,000 homestead exemption. If you are behind and thinking of selling, a sale that pays the tax at closing ends the lien problem before a lawsuit begins.

sections.h2: Does a tax sale affect a seller trying to sell a house?
sections.html:
It does, because a buyer cannot get clear title until the delinquent taxes are paid. A seller with unpaid tax should get a payoff number from the title company and pay the tax from closing funds.

The January 1 owner owes that year's tax, and a suit can still reach that person after a sale. Get the paid-in-full records from the tax office after closing and keep them.

sections.h2: What does the Texas property tax calendar mean for a seller?
sections.html:
Values are fixed on January 1, bills are mailed near October 1, and a split payment lets an owner pay half in November and the balance in June.

Most owners need to pay by January 31, because taxes unpaid on February 1 are delinquent. A bill mailed after January 10 pushes delinquency later, to the first of a month that leaves at least 21 days. For appraisals, the deadline to protest with the appraisal review board is generally May 15, or the 30th day after delivery of the appraisal notice if that comes later. After the board, an owner can appeal to district court, binding arbitration, or the state's administrative hearings office when the board value tops $1,000,000.

  • Residence homestead values may rise no more than 10 percent per year under Section 23.23, starting the year after the exemption is first qualified.
  • Section 11.26 can freeze school tax for an older or disabled homeowner.
  • Appealing owners usually must pay the undisputed amount before the delinquency date.

sections.h2: What help exists for owners who are behind on taxes?
sections.html:
Ask the county tax assessor-collector about installment plans, waivers and exemptions before a suit is filed. Many taxing units contract with the assessor-collector, so one office often handles the bill for several units.

The Comptroller notes that those homeowners can pay delinquent amounts in installments, with a 6 percent charge on the late installment and monthly interest. Disabled veterans may qualify for exemptions from $5,000 to $12,000 depending on their disability rating, and a 100 percent disabled veteran can receive a total exemption on the residence homestead. The Section 11.22 application window can stretch up to five years after the delinquency date.

faqs.q: Is there a redemption period after a Texas tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Homestead, agricultural and mineral interest property has two years from the filing of the purchaser's deed, while other property has until the 180th day.

faqs.q: What premium does a redeeming owner pay?
faqs.a: On homestead, agricultural or mineral interest property it is 25 percent in the first year and 50 percent in the second. For other property it cannot exceed 25 percent.

faqs.q: When does the right to claim leftover sale money end?
faqs.a: Two years from the date of the sale. Claims go through the court that ordered the sale under Tax Code Sections 34.03 and 34.04.

faqs.q: When do Texas property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: In most cases unpaid taxes are delinquent on February 1 after the bill year, and a penalty and interest begin that day.

faqs.q: Where do I find tax sale listings?
faqs.a: There is no statewide list. Check the county clerk and county tax office websites, or call the tax office that bills the property.
